topics.title: What a network is and how it evolved

learn.hook: In 1969 four computers in the USA exchanged their first messages over a network called ARPANET. Today hundreds of millions of Indians are online. Here is how we got from there to here.
points: A computer network is a group of interconnected devices (called nodes or hosts) that can share data and resources. Nodes include computers, phones, printers, servers and routers.
Benefits: resource sharing (one printer or internet line for many users), communication (email, video calls), and data sharing (shared files and databases).
ARPANET (1969), funded by the US Department of Defense's ARPA, was the first network of this kind; it initially linked four university and research computers.

Key milestones: email over networks in the early 1970s; the TCP/IP protocols, developed in the 1970s, became ARPANET's standard in 1983; DNS arrived in 1983; NSFNET (1986) of the US National Science Foundation linked universities and research centres with a faster backbone and helped grow the Internet.
Around 1990 Tim Berners-Lee at CERN created the World Wide Web, along with HTML and URLs, which made the Internet easy for everyone to use.

example.q: Arrange in order: NSFNET, ARPANET, World Wide Web.
steps: ARPANET came first, in 1969

The World Wide Web came about 1990

topics.title: Types of networks: PAN, LAN, MAN and WAN

learn.hook: Your earbuds and phone form a network. So does the entire Internet. The difference is mostly about distance.
points: PAN (Personal Area Network): devices around one person, within a few metres (about 10 m), e.g. a phone linked to earbuds, a smartwatch or a laptop by Bluetooth or USB.
LAN (Local Area Network): computers in a single room, building or campus, such as a school lab or an office. It is privately owned, fast and has few errors.
MAN (Metropolitan Area Network): spreads across a city or town, e.g. a cable TV network or a city-wide network of bank branches.
WAN (Wide Area Network): spans states, countries or continents, often by joining many LANs and MANs. The Internet is the largest WAN.
Order by area covered: PAN < LAN < MAN < WAN.

example.q: Classify: (a) a smartwatch synced with a phone, (b) 60 computers in a school building, (c) a cable TV network across Bengaluru, (d) a bank linking branches in 20 states.

(b) one building → LAN

learn.hook: Every case-study question in the board paper asks 'which device, and where?' Learn what each box does and you will answer in seconds.
points: Modem (MOdulator-DEModulator): converts digital signals from a computer into analog signals for a telephone or cable line (modulation), and back again (demodulation).

Ethernet card or NIC (Network Interface Card): lets a computer connect to a wired network; each NIC has a unique MAC address. An RJ45 is an 8-pin connector used with twisted-pair Ethernet cables. A Wi-Fi card does the same job wirelessly.
Repeater: regenerates (amplifies and restores) a weakened signal so it can travel farther. Signals on Ethernet cable weaken after about 100 m.

Hub: connects many devices but sends incoming data to ALL its ports (broadcast). Switch: also connects devices, but forwards data only to the intended device, using MAC addresses, which cuts unnecessary traffic.

Router: connects different networks (for example a LAN to the Internet) and finds the best route for packets using IP addresses. Gateway: the entry and exit point of a network, able to connect networks that use different protocols. A Wi-Fi access point lets wireless devices join a wired LAN.

example.q: An office LAN of 25 PCs must share one broadband connection. Which devices are needed?
steps: Each PC needs a NIC (or Wi-Fi card)
A switch joins all 25 PCs into one LAN
A router (often combined with a modem) connects the LAN to the ISP and the Internet
example.answer: NICs, a switch, and a router/modem

learn.hook: If one cable snaps, does your whole office go offline or just one desk? The answer depends on the topology.
points: Topology is the arrangement of nodes and links in a network. Mesh: every node is connected to every other node. n nodes need n(n - 1)/2 links. Very reliable, but costly and hard to cable.
Ring: each node connects to exactly two neighbours, forming a closed loop; data usually travels in one direction. A single break can disrupt the whole ring.
Bus: all nodes share one backbone cable with terminators at the ends. Cheap and needs the least cable, but a fault in the backbone stops the whole network, and faults are hard to find.

Star: every node connects to a central hub or switch. Easy to install, extend and troubleshoot; one node's failure does not affect others, but if the central device fails, the whole network stops. Uses more cable than bus.

Tree (hierarchical): star networks joined by a bus-like backbone, as in a school with a switch on each floor. Choosing a layout in case studies: usually a star from the server building, which keeps cable short and failures contained.

example.q: How many direct links does a fully connected mesh of 6 computers need?
steps: Each of 6 nodes connects to 5 others: 6 × 5 = 30 ends
Each link is counted twice, so divide by 2

topics.title: MAC and IP addresses, the Internet, the Web, IoT and DNS

learn.hook: You type ncert.nic.in, but computers only understand numbers like 164.100.x.x. A hidden phone book called DNS makes the switch in milliseconds.
points: MAC address: the unique 48-bit (6-byte) physical address burnt into a NIC, written as 12 hexadecimal digits in six pairs, e.g. 30-9C-23-1B-83-A5. The first half identifies the manufacturer. It does not change when the device moves.

IP address: a logical address given to a device on a network, which can change when it joins another network. IPv4 uses 32 bits written as four numbers from 0 to 255 (192.168.1.10). IPv6 uses 128 bits, written as eight groups of hexadecimal digits, because IPv4 addresses were running out.

The Internet is the global network of networks (the infrastructure). The World Wide Web is one service that runs on it: a collection of linked web pages accessed with browsers. Email and file transfer also use the Internet but are not the Web.
IoT (Internet of Things): everyday objects such as smart meters, ACs, watches and street lights connected to the Internet to send data and be controlled.

A domain name such as www.ncert.nic.in is a readable name for an IP address. The last part is the top-level domain (TLD): generic ones like .com, .org, .edu, .gov, or country codes like .in. DNS (Domain Name System) servers translate domain names into IP addresses; this is called name resolution.

example.q: Arun types www.isro.gov.in in his browser. Outline what happens before the page loads.
steps: The browser asks a DNS server for the IP address of www.isro.gov.in
The DNS server resolves the name and returns the IP address
The browser contacts the web server at that IP address
The server sends the web page back to the browser
example.answer: DNS resolves the name to an IP address, then the browser fetches the page from that server

learn.reallife: Smart electricity meters installed by Indian power distribution companies report usage over the network automatically, a real IoT example in many cities.

quiz.explain: Each of the four numbers must be from 0 to 255. 300 and 256 are too large, and 172.16.5 has only three parts.
steps: IPv4 needs four numbers, each from 0 to 255.
256 and 300 are too large; 172.16.5 has only three parts.
10.0.0.25 is valid.
quiz.mistake: Forgets that each part can be at most 255

quiz.q: What does DNS do?
options: Translates domain names into IP addresses
quiz.explain: DNS servers resolve names such as www.cbse.gov.in to the numeric IP addresses computers use.
steps: Computers use numeric IP addresses; people use domain names.
DNS servers translate domain names into IP addresses (name resolution).
So DNS translates domain names into IP addresses.
Answer: Translates domain names into IP addresses
quiz.mistake: Confuses DNS with web hosting

quiz.q: In the domain name www.cbse.gov.in, what is the top-level domain?
quiz.explain: The top-level domain is the last part: .in, India's country code.
steps: The top-level domain is the last part of a domain name.
In www.cbse.gov.in the last part is .in.
So the TLD is .in.
Answer: .in
quiz.mistake: Reads the domain from left to right and picks the wrong part

quiz.q: Which statement correctly distinguishes the Internet from the World Wide Web?
options: The Web is the hardware, the Internet is the web pages
The Internet is a global network of networks; the Web is a service of linked pages that runs on it
They are two names for the same thing
The Internet works only with email
quiz.explain: The Internet is the infrastructure. The Web is one of the services that uses it, alongside email, file transfer and more.
steps: The Internet is the global network of networks: the infrastructure.
The Web is one service on it: linked pages viewed in browsers.
So they are not the same thing.
Answer: The Internet is a global network of networks; the Web is a service of linked pages that runs on it
quiz.mistake: Uses 'Internet' and 'Web' as synonyms

quiz.q: A smart AC that you can switch on from your phone while travelling home is an example of what?
quiz.explain: An everyday appliance connected to the Internet and controlled remotely is part of the Internet of Things.
steps: The AC is an everyday object connected to the Internet.
It can be controlled remotely from a phone.
That is IoT (Internet of Things).
Answer: IoT
quiz.mistake: Calls any phone connection a PAN

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): A laptop's IP address can change when it moves from home Wi-Fi to the school network.
Reason (R): A MAC address is a 48-bit physical address fixed in the network card.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Both are true. A is true because IP is a logical address given by each network. R is true but describes the MAC address, so it does not explain why the IP address changes.
steps: IP is a logical address given by each network, so it can change: A is true.
A MAC address is a fixed 48-bit physical address: R is true.
But R describes MAC, so it does not explain A.
Answer: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
quiz.mistake: Thinks any true statement about addresses explains A

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Why does my computer need both a MAC address and an IP address?'
teach.praise: Wonderful! The MAC address is the fixed physical address of the network card; the IP address is a logical address given by the network, which can change.
teach.nudge: Which address is fixed in the hardware, and which one is given by the network?

revise.summary: A MAC address is a fixed 48-bit physical address of a NIC; an IP address is a logical address that can change (IPv4 32 bits, IPv6 128 bits). The Web runs on the Internet, IoT connects everyday objects, and DNS translates domain names into IP addresses.
focus: Tell MAC addresses from IP addresses
Recognise valid IPv4 addresses
Distinguish the Internet from the World Wide Web
Explain DNS and top-level domains
remember: MAC: 48 bits, 12 hex digits, fixed in the NIC
IPv4: 32 bits, four numbers 0–255; IPv6: 128 bits
Internet = network of networks; Web = linked pages on it
DNS resolves domain names to IP addresses; TLD is the last part (.in, .com)
traps: Don't accept an IPv4 part above 255
The Internet and the Web are not the same thing
The TLD of www.cbse.gov.in is .in, not .gov

topics.title: Web services: HTML, XML, URLs, browsers, servers and hosting

learn.hook: Every time you open the DigiLocker website, a browser on your phone asks a web server somewhere for an HTML page. Let's open the hood.
points:
WWW: a system of interlinked documents and resources on the Internet. HTML (HyperText Markup Language) uses predefined tags such as

and

to present web pages; it is not case-sensitive.
XML (eXtensible Markup Language) stores and carries data using user-defined tags such as <rollno>; it is case-sensitive and focuses on data rather than display. HTML shows data; XML describes data.

A URL (Uniform Resource Locator) is the address of a resource on the web. In https://www.ncert.nic.in/textbook.php, https is the protocol, www.ncert.nic.in is the domain name and textbook.php is the path to the document.

A web page is a single document on the web; a website is a collection of related web pages under one domain. A web browser (Chrome, Firefox, Edge, Safari) is client software that requests and displays pages; a web server is a computer and software that stores pages and sends them on request.
Web hosting is the service of storing a website's files on a server permanently connected to the Internet, so that anyone can reach the site by its domain name.

example.q: Identify the parts of the URL https://www.cbse.gov.in/results.html.
steps: Protocol: https
Domain name: www.cbse.gov.in
Path / document: results.html

learn.reallife: An Indian startup launching its website pays a hosting company to keep its pages on servers that run all day and night, so customers from Kashmir to Kanyakumari can open it at any hour.

Keeping a site's files on an Internet server

quiz.q: In the URL https://www.ncert.nic.in/textbook.php, what is 'https'?
quiz.explain: The part before :// is the protocol used to fetch the resource.
steps: In a URL, the part before :// is the protocol.
Here that part is https.
So https is the protocol.
Answer: Protocol
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the protocol and the domain name

quiz.q: Which is the main difference between HTML and XML?
options: HTML has user-defined tags; XML has predefined tags
XML is used only for images
HTML presents data using predefined tags; XML stores and carries data using user-defined tags
quiz.explain: HTML focuses on how content looks; XML describes what the data is, with tags you invent.
steps:
HTML uses predefined tags like

to present data.
XML uses user-defined tags like <rollno> to store and carry data.
So HTML presents data; XML stores and carries it.
Answer: HTML presents data using predefined tags; XML stores and carries data using user-defined tags
quiz.mistake: Swaps the tag rules of HTML and XML

quiz.q: Which of these is a web browser?
quiz.explain: Firefox is client software for viewing web pages. Apache is web server software and MySQL is a DBMS.
steps: A web browser is client software that displays web pages.
Firefox is a browser; Apache is a web server; MySQL is a DBMS; Python is a language.
So the browser is Mozilla Firefox.
Answer: Mozilla Firefox
quiz.mistake: Confuses a web server program with a browser

quiz.q: What is web hosting?
options: Converting domain names to IP addresses
Storing a website's files on a server connected to the Internet so it can be accessed
Designing a web page in HTML
quiz.explain: A hosting provider keeps the site's files on servers that are always online.
steps: Web hosting stores a website's files on a server.
The server is always connected to the Internet.
So anyone can reach the site by its domain name.
Answer: Storing a website's files on a server connected to the Internet so it can be accessed
quiz.mistake: Confuses hosting with DNS or design

quiz.q: What is the difference between a web page and a website?
options: A web page is always on a local computer
A website is a single document; a web page is a collection
A web page is a single document; a website is a collection of related web pages
quiz.explain: A website groups many related pages under one domain.
steps: A web page is one document on the web.
A website is a collection of related web pages under one domain.
So a web page is a single document; a website is a collection.
Answer: A web page is a single document; a website is a collection of related web pages
quiz.mistake: Reverses the two terms

quiz.q: Which statement about XML is TRUE?
options: Its tags are fixed by the language
It is used mainly to decide the colours of a web page
quiz.explain: XML tags are user-defined and case-sensitive, so <Name> and <name> are different.
steps: XML tags are user-defined.
XML is case-sensitive: <Name> and <name> are different.
So 'It is case-sensitive' is true.
Answer: It is case-sensitive
quiz.mistake: Assumes XML behaves like HTML

quiz.q: What is the role of a web server?
options: Display web pages on the user's screen
Store web pages and send them to browsers on request
quiz.explain: Browsers request pages; web servers store and deliver them.
steps: Browsers request web pages.
Web servers store the pages and send them on request.
So that is the role of a web server.
Answer: Store web pages and send them to browsers on request
quiz.mistake: Confuses the server's role with the browser's

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): XML is called 'extensible'.
Reason (R): In XML, users can define their own tags.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Because you can create new tags to suit your data, the language can be extended. R explains A.
steps: In XML, users can define their own tags (R is true).
So the language can be extended: it is 'extensible' (A is true).
R explains A.
Answer: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
quiz.mistake: Does not link user-defined tags to 'extensible'

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'What are the parts of a URL like https://www.cbse.gov.in/index.html?'
teach.praise: Perfect! A URL has the protocol, the domain name and the path to the document.
teach.nudge: What does the part before :// tell us, what is the name of the site, and what comes after the slash?

revise.summary: The WWW is a system of linked documents. HTML presents data with predefined tags, XML stores data with user-defined, case-sensitive tags, a URL gives a resource's address, browsers request pages from web servers, and hosting keeps sites online.
focus: Compare HTML and XML
Identify the parts of a URL
Tell a web page from a website, and a browser from a server
Explain web hosting
remember: HTML: predefined tags, presents data, not case-sensitive
XML: user-defined tags, describes data, case-sensitive ('extensible')
URL parts: protocol (https), domain name, path
Browser requests pages; web server stores and sends them; hosting keeps files on an online server
traps: Don't swap the tag rules of HTML and XML
Don't mix up a website (many pages) with a web page (one)
Apache is web server software, not a browser

learn.hook: Section E of the board paper almost always describes a company with four buildings and asks you to design its network. There is a reliable method. Here it is.
points: Server location: put the server in the building with the MOST computers. That keeps most traffic inside one building (the 80-20 rule of thumb) and reduces cabling.
Cable layout: usually a star from the server building to every other building, which keeps cable short and failures contained. Write it as a simple diagram.
Repeater: place one on any cable run longer than about 100 m (Ethernet's limit). Hub or switch: one in EVERY building, to connect its computers. A switch is preferred over a hub.

Joining distant sites: within a campus use Ethernet cable or optical fibre; across hilly or distant places (hundreds of km) use satellite, microwave or radio links. Network type: buildings within a campus form a LAN; offices in different cities form a WAN.
Common difference questions: hub vs switch, LAN vs WAN, MAC vs IP, circuit vs packet switching, and matching each device to its function.

example.q: A school has four blocks with these computer counts: Admin 30, Science 90, Junior 40, Library 15. Distances from Science: Admin 120 m, Junior 80 m, Library 60 m. Where do the server and repeaters go?
steps: The Science block has the most computers (90), so the server goes there
Use a star layout from Science to the other three blocks
Only the Science–Admin run (120 m) is longer than 100 m, so place a repeater on it
Put a switch in every block
example.answer: Server in Science; repeater on the Science–Admin link; a switch in each block

learn.reallife: Large Indian hospitals such as AIIMS run campus networks linking OPD blocks, labs and wards. Planners follow exactly these rules to decide where the main server and switches go.

games.title: Network design checklist
games.prompt: In the order you usually answer
items: Find the building with the most computers
Place the server there
Draw a star cable layout from that building

Put a switch in every building

games.title: Match the situation to the best choice
pairs: Link of 150 m on Ethernet cable
Office in a remote hilly area

quiz.q: A company has four blocks with these numbers of computers: A 25, B 110, C 40, D 15. Where should the server be placed?
quiz.explain: Block B has the most computers, so most traffic stays local and cabling is minimised.
steps: The server should go in the building with the most computers.
Counts: A 25, B 110, C 40, D 15.
B has the most, so Block B.
Answer: Block B
quiz.mistake: Picks a block because it is in the middle, ignoring the number of computers

quiz.q: In a campus, the distances from the server block are P 70 m, Q 130 m and R 90 m. On which link is a repeater required?
quiz.explain: Only the 130 m run exceeds about 100 m, beyond which Ethernet signals weaken too much.
steps: A repeater is needed on cable runs longer than about 100 m.
P 70 m and R 90 m are within the limit; Q is 130 m.
So a repeater is required on the server-to-Q link.
Answer: Server to Q
quiz.mistake: Puts repeaters on every link

quiz.q: Which device should be installed in each building of a campus to connect the computers inside it?
quiz.explain: A switch connects all the computers within a building into the LAN.
steps: Each building needs a device to connect its computers into the LAN.
A switch does this (and is preferred over a hub).
So a switch.
Answer: Switch
quiz.mistake: Chooses a modem, which only links to a phone or cable line

quiz.q: A company in Mumbai opens a branch in a remote hill town about 900 km away, where laying cable is impractical. What is the best way to connect them?
quiz.explain: For long distances over difficult terrain, satellite (or microwave) links are used.
steps: 900 km over hilly ground makes cables impractical.
Bluetooth and infrared are very short-range.
A satellite link suits long distances over difficult terrain.
Answer: Satellite link
quiz.mistake: Chooses short-range wireless like Bluetooth or infrared

quiz.q: A company's four buildings on one campus are networked together. What type of network is this?
quiz.explain: Buildings within a single campus form a LAN.
steps: All four buildings are on one campus.
Buildings within a campus form a LAN.
So it is a LAN.
Answer: LAN
quiz.mistake: Calls a multi-building network a WAN

quiz.q: Which cable layout is usually suggested for connecting all buildings to the server building?
options: Star layout from the server building
A single bus with no switches
quiz.explain: A star from the server building keeps each link independent, so a cable fault affects only one building.
steps: A star from the server building gives each building its own link.
Short cables, and a fault affects only one building.
So a star layout from the server building.
Answer: Star layout from the server building
quiz.mistake: Prefers a ring or bus, where a single break affects many buildings

quiz.q: A university wants to connect two campus buildings 400 m apart with high speed and immunity to electrical interference. Which medium is best?
quiz.explain: Optical fibre carries light, so it has very high bandwidth, low loss over distance and no electromagnetic interference.
steps: 400 m is too far for Ethernet cable without repeaters, and wireless options here are short-range.
Optical fibre carries light: high speed, low loss, no electrical interference.
So optical fibre.
Answer: Optical fibre
quiz.mistake: Picks a wireless option meant for very short ranges

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): In a network case study, the server is usually placed in the building with the most computers.
Reason (R): Placing it there keeps most network traffic within one building and reduces cabling.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Most requests come from that building, so traffic and cable runs are minimised. R explains A.
steps: Most requests come from the building with the most computers (R is true).
Placing the server there keeps traffic local and reduces cabling (A is true).
R explains A.
Answer: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
quiz.mistake: Thinks the server should go in the smallest building

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'In a network case study, how do I decide where to put the server?'
teach.praise: Smart! Place the server where the most computers are, to keep traffic local and cabling short.
teach.nudge: Which building should get the server, and why does that help?

revise.summary: In network case studies, place the server in the building with the most computers, use a star layout from it, add repeaters on runs over about 100 m and a switch in every building, and choose media like optical fibre or satellite based on distance.
focus: Choose the server building
Decide where repeaters and switches go
Suggest a cable layout
Choose a transmission medium and network type
remember: Server in the building with the most computers
Star layout from the server building
Repeater on runs longer than about 100 m; switch in every building
Campus → LAN; cities → WAN; far, hilly places → satellite or microwave; high speed, no interference → optical fibre
traps: Don't put the server in the middle building by default
Don't put repeaters on every link
Don't choose Bluetooth or infrared for long distances; they are very short-range
